lessons.title: The first thirty seconds
lessons.text:
The first half minute decides whether you get a second one. It is also the part the law cares about.

# Say who, for whom and why, inside thirty seconds
Colorado makes it a deceptive trade practice to sell door to door unless, within thirty seconds of starting the conversation, you say who you are, who you represent and why you are there. Opening with a question ("Are you the homeowner?") is the easy way to fail it. Lead with the three facts.

# SEE: how you say it
- Smile. It is contagious, and it tells them you are not a problem.
- Eye contact. It builds trust and shows you believe what you are saying.
- Enthusiasm. It makes them curious about what comes next.

# WWW, kept short and simple
- Who we are: "Hi, I'm ___ with Sixfold."
- What we are doing: what Sixfold is doing around here.
- Why we are doing it: the reason it matters to their place, now.

Keep it short and simple. Two sentences, then stop and let them answer.

# Openers that do all three
- Lawn: "Hi, I'm ___ with Sixfold. We're booking fall aeration in this neighbourhood, and I'm stopping by to see if your lawn's on the list."
- Landscaping: "Hi, I'm ___ with Sixfold. We do landscaping and lawn care around here, and I'm letting neighbours know we have openings this month."
- Fire: "Hi, I'm ___ with Sixfold. We do wildfire mitigation as well as lawn work, and I'm stopping by about the trees close to the houses on this street."

Only say "we're working on this street" or "your neighbours booked" when it is true today. If it isn't, say "in this neighbourhood".

lessons.title: Working the territory
lessons.text:
# Talk to everyone
It is a numbers game. You cannot tell from the truck, the paint or the yard who will say yes, so don't pre-judge and don't cherry-pick. The door you skip is often the one that would have booked.

# Work it in order
- Knock the neighbourhood in street order. The app opens the next door for you.
- Mark every door you knock, even a no answer. A door with no mark looks untouched to the next person, and it gets knocked twice.
- Finish a street before you jump to the next one.

# Who you don't knock
Talking to everyone stops at three things:
- A "No Soliciting" sign. Mark it and move on (see No soliciting).
- A neighbourhood the app flags as no-soliciting.
- Someone who already said no today, or asked us not to come back.

lessons.title: Your day: goals, numbers and attitude
lessons.text:
# Goals
Most doors will say no. That is normal, not a sign you are doing it wrong. Set your own goal for the day in the app (Daily goal) and work to it. How long you work and when is your call.

# Ratios
Your own numbers in the app show how many doors you knocked, how many answered and how many booked. Watch your ratio, not one bad street. Sixfold has no target ratio yet; your numbers over a few weeks will set one.

# Attitude
Attitude does most of the work, ability a little, luck none. There is no bad weather, bad street or bad day that a good attitude does not improve. Every no brings you closer to a yes. Protect your attitude from the last door: the next homeowner didn't hear it.

# Consistency
The pitch stays the same. How you deliver it changes with the person in front of you. Work the system: the five steps, the objection answers, the closing circle.

# Be the person who shows up
- Be early for any walk you booked. Early is on time.
- Be prepared: phone charged, cards and flyers, water, the walk sheet.
- Know why you are out there: your goal for the day and what you want to learn.
- Take control of the conversation, of your day and of what you do next.

lessons.title: No soliciting: three levels
lessons.text:
There are three kinds of "no soliciting". The app can handle two of them.

# The door
A "No Soliciting" sign on one house. Don't knock. Mark it in the app (Not now, then flag the sign) so nobody else knocks it either. In some places ignoring the sign is trespass, not just bad manners.

# The neighbourhood
An HOA or gated community that posts it at the entrance. The app can flag a whole neighbourhood so the crew avoids it. If you see a sign the app doesn't know about, flag it.

# The town
Some towns require a permit for each person who sells door to door. That is the one that can bring a fine, and the app cannot check it for you. Before you work a town Sixfold hasn't worked before, ask the office whether a permit is needed.

lessons.title: The five steps
lessons.text:
Every good door conversation runs the same five steps, in order.

# 1. Introduction
First impression, lasting impression. SEE: smile, eye contact, enthusiasm. Say who you are, that you're with Sixfold and why you're there inside thirty seconds (see The first thirty seconds).

# 2. Short story
Who we are, what we're doing, why we're doing it. Keep it short and simple: two sentences, then let them talk.

# 3. Presentation
- Make it about their place. Look at their lawn, their trees or their yard with them, not at a brochure.
- Put something in their hands: your card or the flyer. Holding it gives them a feeling of ownership.
- Package it: aeration, overseed and fertilizer in one visit, with the machine, seed and fertilizer brought by us.
- Speak like a professional: "dollars", not "bucks".
- We don't give a price at the door. Every lawn and every lot is different, so someone walks it and the office gives a fixed price. That walk is what you are selling.

# 4. Close
- Ask questions they will say yes to: "You'd like the lawn thicker next spring?" "Mornings or afternoons are easier?"
- Assume the booking: "I can have someone walk it Thursday afternoon or Saturday morning. Which is better?"
- Close with confidence. Always be closing.

The close at the door is a booked walk. Tap Quote booked and book the walk while you're standing there.

# 5. Rehash
Once the walk is booked, offer the second thing: overseed with the aeration, monthly care, the trees close to the house. Never stop at the first yes. See Adding the second service.

lessons.title: Objections: AIR and FFF
lessons.text:
A negative comment is not a no. Two ways to answer one:

# Agree, Ignore, Resume (AIR)
"I totally understand. Anyway, what I wanted to show you is..." and go back to your point.

# Feel, Felt, Found (FFF)
"I hear you. My last neighbour felt the same way until they found out..." and give one true fact. Only use "my last neighbour" when it happened.

# What people say, and what's true to say back
- "I'm in a hurry." "I'll be fifteen seconds, for next time."
- "How much is it?" "Every lawn's different, so we don't guess at the door. We walk it and you get a fixed price, and the quote's free."
- "I do it myself." "Plenty of people do. The difference is we bring the machine, the seed and the fertilizer, and it's done in one visit."
- "I already have a guy." "Good. If he doesn't aerate, we can do just that part."
- "I need to ask my spouse." "Wouldn't want to get in the way. Let's book the walk for when you're both home, and they can ask me anything then."
- "Not now." "No problem. Spring or fall?" Then mark Not now with that come-back date.
- "We're under water restrictions." "Aeration still works on your watering days: water the day before and soon after. Which water provider are you on?" (See Water, wells and seed.)
- "I'm on a well." "Do you know what your well permit allows for the lawn?" If it's household use only, sell aeration on a green lawn, mowing or cleanup, not seed.
- "Will the seed come up? Do you guarantee it?" "We don't guarantee germination, because it depends on water and weather. We'll do the aeration, seed and feed properly and tell you exactly how to water it."
- "Can you spray the weeds while you're here?" "We don't apply weed killer or any pesticide."
- "Is this legit?" "Fair question. Here's my card. Look us up at sixfoldcolorado.com, or call the number on it."

lessons.title: The closing circle
lessons.text:
A no at the door is usually a "not yet". The closing circle is how you keep the conversation moving without arguing.

# The circle
- Objection: they give you a reason.
- AIR or FFF: agree, then move on or tell what others found.
- Rebuttal: one true fact that answers the reason.
- Popularity: what people around here are choosing (only if true).
- Real urgency: the season, the schedule, their watering days (only if true).
- What they'd miss: a thin lawn next spring, the gap in the schedule (only if true).
- Close: ask for the booking again.
- Rehash: once they say yes, offer the second service.

Then round again. Don't stop at the first no.

# When the circle stops
- A clear, firm no.
- They step back and start closing the door.
- They ask you to leave.
Thank them, leave a card if they'll take one, mark the door and go. Never argue.

lessons.title: Building value honestly: GIFTS
lessons.text:
GIFTS is how you make what we do feel worth it. Every line has to be true.

# G: what everyone else is doing
People want what their neighbours have. "Most people on this side of town aerate in the fall." "Our most popular add-on is the overseed." Say it only when it's true. Point at the house down the street only if you really did that house.

# I: indifference
Be the opposite of a pushy salesperson. Nobody wants to be sold. "It's up to you." "You don't have to decide today." Relax, step back, let them come to you.

# F: what they'd lose
People hate losing something more than they like gaining it. Use what is real: the fall window for aeration closes when the ground freezes; this week's openings fill; seed down too late may not take this year. Never say "last day", "sold out" or "price goes up tomorrow" unless it's true. A made-up deadline or shortage can be a deceptive trade practice under Colorado law.

# T: tone
It's not just what you say, it's how you say it. The same words land differently said calm, warm and sure than said fast and loud.

# S: sense of urgency
Move with purpose. "Super quick." "Two seconds." Get the phone out and start booking while you're talking. Action beats hesitation.

lessons.title: Adding the second service
lessons.text:
# 1. Secure the first yes
The walk is booked in the app, or the agreement is signed. Never start on the second service before the first one is secure.

# 2. Thank them and say what they did
"Thanks. You're down for Thursday, and someone will walk the lawn and give you a fixed price."

# 3. Segue
"While I've got you..." or "You don't hit home runs if you don't swing, right?"

# 4. Rebuild the reason
Give one or two true points about the second service. For example:
- Overseed: "Aerating opens the soil, and that's the best time to get seed into it."
- Monthly care: mowing, feeding and snow clearing on a monthly plan.
- Trees: "Those two spruce are right against the house. We do wildfire mitigation as well, if you ever want someone to look."
- Landscaping: beds, cleanup and planting, as its own job.

# 5. Ask
Offer two options, matched to their tone. "Do you want the seed with it, or just the aeration?" Then stop talking.

# 6. Close on a no
If they say no to the bigger option, offer one smaller step: "Want me to have them look at the trees while they're walking the lawn? No charge to look."

lessons.title: Do's and don'ts
lessons.text:
# Do
- Sell with integrity.
- Think long term: offer monthly care where it fits. The standard lawn plan is month to month.
- Close more than once. Use the closing circle.
- Mark every door in the app, the same day.
- Rehash everyone who says yes.
- Get the details right on every booking: name, phone, the walk day.

# Don't
- Ever skip telling someone who signs that they can cancel within three business days. Say it out loud. The law requires it (see Signing at the door).
- Misrepresent Sixfold or what we do.
- Argue with anyone.
- Send them to the website unless they ask.
- Rehash before the first yes is secure.
- Swear.
- Be creepy, needy or pushy.

lessons.title: What we never say
lessons.text:
Some things sound helpful and get Sixfold in trouble. Don't say them, even as a joke.

# About Sixfold
- Never say licensed, insured, bonded, certified or Firewise.
- Never say we'll beat someone's price, or quote a competitor's.

# About money
- Never give a price at the door. There is no flat aeration price: the walk sets it.
- Never promise a tax credit amount, a refund or an insurance discount.
- Never name a county cost-share programme as if Sixfold is on its approved list.
- Call the first half a "first payment", never a "deposit".

# About the work
- Never promise the seed will come up. We don't guarantee germination.
- Never promise watering. We can water the ground in on the day, with the owner's own system. After that it's theirs.
- Never offer weed killer, weed and feed or any pesticide.
- Never agree to extra work by word of mouth. Changes go on a signed change order first.

# About landscaping
Landscaping is a service on its own. Never call it the cleanup after fire mitigation. "Book one, or book them together."

lessons.title: Water, wells and seed
lessons.text:
# The one thing to know
Aeration needs a green, watered lawn. Overseeding needs much more water. If a customer can only water two or three days a week, an overseed may not take, and we don't water and don't guarantee germination.

# Ask on every lawn
"Which water provider are you on?" One question, and it changes what we should sell.

# Say
- "Aeration still works on your watering days: water the day before and soon after."
- "Water the lawn a day or two before we come out."
- On Colorado Springs Utilities: "There's a permit that lets you water more often while new seed comes in. I can tell you how to get it."

# Wells
A well is not a way around the rules. Most wells on lots under 35 acres are household use only, and can't legally water a lawn at all. Ask what the well permit allows before offering seed. If it's household use only, sell aeration on a green lawn, mowing or cleanup.

# Don't
- Promise the seed will come up.
- Quote a watering schedule without checking it that week.
- Say "you're on a well, so the restrictions don't apply."
- Aerate a lawn that's brown and dormant from water restrictions.

lessons.title: Walking a lawn
lessons.text:
The walk is where the job is won or lost. Walk the lawn with the owner if you can.

# Ask
- Which water provider are they on? (City utility, a district, or a well.)
- On a well: what does the permit allow? Household use only means no lawn watering at all.
- Is the lawn green, or brown and dormant? Don't aerate a dormant lawn.
- What do they want: aeration only, or with overseed and fertilizer?

# Look for
- Sprinkler heads, valve boxes and invisible pet fence. Get the owner to point them out. Private lines that aren't marked are theirs to show us.
- Septic tank and leach field, a well head, buried propane, low-voltage lighting.
- Slopes, rock, tight gates and anything the machine can't reach.
- Beds, new planting or bare ground they want left alone.

# Tell them
- The plugs stay on the lawn and break down in a few weeks. That's how it's meant to work.
- Water the lawn a day or two before we come. Dry, hard ground gives a poor plug.
- We request utility locates through Colorado 811 before the job, so the date allows for that.

# Record it
Use the walk in the app or the walk sheet. Write what you saw, not a price.

lessons.title: Walking a tree or clearing job
lessons.text:
Use the quote walk sheet: on the phone (the fillable PDF works with no signal) or printed. It has no prices on it, on purpose.

# Section 1: count what gets charged
- Trees to take down, in the height bands on the sheet.
- How many of those come down over a roof, fence, line or drive. This is the row that turns a one-cut tree into a piece-by-piece removal, and it doesn't show in a tree count.
- Trees to limb instead of remove.
- Logs to buck, and the round length.
- Dead fall, brush, branches.
- Chipper hours, slash piles to build.
- Stumps: how many, and the diameter at the ground with the root flare. One that looks 14 inches at eye level is often 22 at the soil.
- Loads to haul off. Count the pile twice and write both counts: it's the number that moves the cost most and is got wrong most.
- What stays on site instead.

# Section 2: what the job takes
- Crew people and days.
- Chains, gas, mix and bar oil.
- Chipper, trailer, stump grinder: ours or rented, and the rental cost.
- Dump fees per load: call and confirm today's figure.
- Truck trips, and whether a second trip is needed (the 811 locate is the usual reason).

# Section 3: notes
Everything else that will change the job. If it surprised you, write it down.

lessons.title: Prices: the office sets them
lessons.text:
# The rule
You count. The office prices. The Quote builder in the app turns the counts into a price, and only admins use it.

# Never
- Never give a price at the door or on the walk. There's no flat aeration rate: every lawn is quoted from its walk.
- Never fill in a price the office hasn't agreed.
- Never leave a signed agreement with the price blank.
- Never quote from an old price sheet or from memory.

# What the customer gets
- A fixed price for the work written on the agreement. Travel isn't billed.
- For aeration, the seed, fertilizer and machine are inside the price.
- Payment in two halves: the first payment on or before the first day of work, the rest when the work is done. Call it the "first payment", never a "deposit".
- Anything extra goes on a signed change order before the work, or it isn't owed.

lessons.title: Jobs we don't take, or call in first
lessons.text:
Some things stop a quote on the spot. Say "I'll have the office call you about that part" and move on.

# Not a Sixfold job
- Any tree touching, leaning toward or within 10 feet of a power line, until the utility has made it safe. We have no line-clearance qualified crew.
- Anything that needs climbing, a ladder in a tree or a lift. We work from the ground.
- Weed spraying or any pesticide. We aren't licensed to apply them.
- In Colorado Springs city limits: cutting, pruning, shaping or removing any tree 15 feet or taller. The city requires a tree service licence for that, and Sixfold doesn't hold one.

# Call the office first
- A tree over 80 feet.
- Stump grinding or digging: Colorado 811 needs at least two business days' notice before any ground disturbance, so it can't be same-day.

lessons.title: Answering the phone
lessons.text:
# Pick up like this
"Sixfold, this is ___." Warm, unhurried, and smiling: they can hear it.

# Get five things
- Their name.
- The address of the property.
- What they want done: lawn, landscaping, trees or fire.
- For a lawn: which water provider they're on, or whether they're on a well.
- The best number and time to reach them.

# Then book the walk
The phone close is the same as the door close: a booked walk. "I can have someone out Thursday afternoon or Saturday morning. Which works?" An admin adds them in the Pipeline with + Add a lead (the Pipeline is admin-only, so if that isn't you, pass the five things to the office the same day), and the walk goes on the calendar.

# What not to do on the phone
- Don't give a price. "Every property's different, so we walk it and give you a fixed price. The quote's free."
- Don't promise a date for the work itself until the office has priced it.
- Don't send an agreement off a phone call. The price comes off a walk.

lessons.title: Where leads come in, and who picks them up
lessons.text:
# The four ways in
- The website form: lands in the app's Pipeline by itself and is emailed to Contact@.
- Facebook / Instagram ad forms: land in Meta's Leads Center, not in email. An admin downloads them and uses Import leads from Meta in the Pipeline. Someone has to check Leads Center every day, or those people wait.
- Phone calls, Nextdoor messages and referrals: an admin adds them by hand in the Pipeline with + Add a lead.
- Doors: a Quote booked at the door goes into the Pipeline by itself.

# Every lead needs an owner
A new lead belongs to nobody until an admin (in the Pipeline) or a manager (in Leads) gives it an owner. Then it shows in that person's My leads, where they call or text, move its status and set a follow-up date that goes on their calendar.

# A message is not a lead
A Facebook message or a comment asking a question isn't booked work. Answer it, get the five things, and add it as a lead.

lessons.title: Calling a lead back
lessons.text:
# Call fast
Someone who just filled in a form is thinking about it now. Call the same day if you can.

# Say who, for whom and why
Same as the door: "Hi, this is ___ with Sixfold. You asked about aeration on our website, so I'm calling to set up a time to look at the lawn."

# Calling hours
Only between 8 am and 9 pm, their time.

# Do Not Call: whose number is it?
- They gave us the number (a form, a call, at the door): call them.
- We looked the number up ourselves (Look up number): the app marks it "looked up" and warns that it has to clear the national and Colorado Do Not Call lists first. The app doesn't check those lists for you. Until the office has checked the number, don't call it: knock or send a letter instead.
- Anyone who says "don't call me again": stop, and note it on the lead.

# Texts
Only text a number the person gave us. The app's Text a confirmation does exactly that after a booking.

lessons.title: Voicemail
lessons.text:
Keep it under twenty seconds:
- Who you are and that you're with Sixfold.
- Why you're calling, in one line ("about the lawn aeration you asked about").
- The number, said twice, slowly: (303) 915-1045.

Then set a follow-up on the lead so you try again in a day or two. One more try is enough unless they call back.

lessons.title: Signing at the door
lessons.text:
# Why this matters
If the customer cancels inside the window, Sixfold gets nothing for work already done. And if the cancellation forms are missing, wrong or left blank, the three days never start: the customer can cancel for three years, still with nothing owed for the work.

# Before you hand the paperwork over
- Date it the day they actually sign. Not the day you walked it or wrote the quote.
- Work out the deadline: midnight of the third business day after signing. Business days are every day except Sunday and federal holidays, so Saturday counts.
- Write the deadline in three places: page 2 section 6, and both cancellation forms.
- Fill in both cancellation forms yourself: seller name, seller address, date of the transaction, deadline. The law says we fill these in, not the customer.

# As they sign
Say it out loud: "You have three business days to change your mind, and these forms are how." Pointing at the box isn't enough.

# After
- Leave them a signed copy of every page and both cancellation forms.
- Never ask anyone to give up the right to cancel. Asking is itself a violation.
- If they cancel: refund everything within ten days, no deductions, and tell the office that day.

lessons.title: Starting work and the three-day window
lessons.text:
# You can start, but it's at our risk
Nothing stops work starting the same day. But if they cancel inside the window, we refund everything and are paid nothing for the work done. So plan the job so the window costs least.

# What to do first, and what to hold back
- Do first: work we'd be repeating anyway, like hand work and clearing close to the house.
- Hold back: anything we can't get back. Haul-off, chipping, stump grinding.
- Stump grinding can't be same-day anyway: Colorado 811 needs two business days' notice before digging.

# The emergency exception is narrow
All three must be true:
- The customer contacted us. If we knocked, it doesn't apply.
- There's a real emergency at this property: a hazard tree over a bedroom, storm damage. Not "before the party", not fire season in general.
- They write the statement themselves, by hand, dated and signed: what the emergency is, why it can't wait, that they want us to start now, and that they know they're giving up the three days. No form, no dictating.
If you're talking someone into calling it an emergency, it isn't one.

lessons.title: Sending an agreement to sign
lessons.text:
Everything about signing at the door still applies. Two things get harder when you're not in the room.

# Agree the signing day first
On the phone, agree a day. The deadline depends on the day they sign, and you don't control it. If in doubt, write a later deadline, never an earlier one: a window that's too long is fine, one that's too short is the defect.

# Fill it in completely, then send
Price, scope, the date, section 6 and both cancellation forms. Send every page, never a blank template.

# Be on the phone while they sign
Say it out loud: "Before you sign: you have three business days to change your mind, and the two cancellation forms in there are how you do it." Then note on the job that you said it, and when.

# In DocuSign
- Don't put any signing boxes on the two cancellation form pages. Tagged, DocuSign would make them sign their own cancellation to finish.
- Download the signed copy and the certificate of completion into the job file. The certificate proves when they signed.
- If they signed later than the day you agreed, the deadline you wrote is too short: void it and send again.

# Don't send one at all when
- Nobody has walked the property.
- The office hasn't agreed the price.
- They want work to start immediately. That's a conversation (see Starting work).

lessons.title: Getting paid
lessons.text:
# Two halves
- First payment: half the fixed price, on or before the first day of work.
- The rest: when the work is done.

# Words matter
Call it the "first payment", never a "deposit". The aeration agreements never use the word: the first payment is due on or before the first day of work, and nothing is taken at signing. An invoice that says "deposit" contradicts them.

# What the money can and can't do
The first payment holds the date. It doesn't change their right to cancel: if they cancel inside the window, it comes back in full.

# How they pay
Electronic transfer, cash, or a check made out to Sixfold, LLC.

lessons.title: Every job
lessons.text:
# Protective gear
- Eye protection with saws, chippers, trimmers and edgers.
- Hearing protection whenever a saw, the chipper or a mower is running.
- Gloves, and head, foot and leg protection (chaps) on saw work.
Sixfold provides the protective gear. Ask if you don't have it.

# First aid
- Every crew must have at least one person with current first-aid training. If yours doesn't, say so before the job starts.
- A stocked first-aid kit must be on the truck, with trauma dressings and a tourniquet for saw work.
- Gloves in the kit, and the first-aider uses them.

# Machines and fuel
- Guards stay on. The mower's discharge chute guard is never removed.
- Refuel with the engine off and cooled, no smoking, on bare ground, not in the slash.
- Fuel in approved safety cans, closed, out of the sun, not in the cab.
- A charged fire extinguisher on the truck, next to the fuel.

lessons.title: Saws, chippers, lines and heights
lessons.text:
# Power lines
Any tree touching, leaning toward or within 10 feet of a power line is not ours until the utility has made it safe. No exceptions, no "just this branch".

# Heights
No climbing, no ladder work in trees, no lifts. Everything is felled from the ground. Anything over 80 feet: call the office first.

# Digging and grinding
Before any stump grinding or digging, Colorado 811 must be notified at least two business days ahead, not counting the day you call.

# If you're unsure
Stop and call. A job that waits a day costs nothing next to an injury.

lessons.title: If someone gets hurt
lessons.text:
# The first minutes
- Stop the saw.
- The first-aider takes over.
- A deep cut: direct pressure, a tourniquet if it won't stop, call 911.
- Don't move someone who has fallen.
- Don't drive them yourself if 911 can get there faster.

# Then
- Call the office straight away. Some injuries have to be reported to OSHA within hours, and the office makes that call.
- Write down what happened, when, who was there and what we'll change. It's the record if anything is questioned later.

lessons.title: A day at the doors
lessons.text:
# Find where to knock
Door rounds opens on Colorado: tap a county, then a town, or tap Nearest town. Pick a neighbourhood. You can sort them by lawn, fire, trees, doors left or nearest.

# Knock in street order
The next door is open at the top; the rest are one line each. Each door shows what we know before you knock: lawn size, trees near the house, fire risk.

# Mark every door
- Quote booked: they want the walk.
- Not now: pick when to come back (a month, three months, spring, fall, a date) or flag a no-soliciting sign.
- No answer: it comes back on the list in two days.
A message offers Undo if you tap the wrong one.

lessons.title: After a yes
lessons.text:
# Book the walk first
After Quote booked, the panel opens with Book the walk: a day, a time or "time to agree", and the walks already booked that day so they don't clash. Then Add to calendar for reminders, and Text a confirmation from your phone.

# Add info
One panel holds the rest. Saved items get a tick.
- Phone and email.
- Photos: only with the owner's OK, and of the property, not people.
- A note.
- Extra work you spotted: gutters, branches over the roof, dead trees, bare lawn, beds.
- The fire check.

# What happens next
The booking appears in the office's Pipeline. When the job is won, the office makes them a customer.

lessons.title: Phone numbers and Do Not Call
lessons.text:
# Two kinds of number
- Given at the door: the person told you. Save it as given.
- Looked up: found by searching. Save it as looked up.
The app records which, because a looked-up number has to clear the Do Not Call lists before anyone calls it.

# Look up number
On a door with no number, Look up number shows the owner of record and the address with Copy buttons, and opens a free people-search page in a new tab. Read it, come back and type the number in yourself. The app never reads those sites for you.

# Texting
Only text a number the person gave you.

lessons.title: No signal
lessons.text:
No signal is fine. Anything you save without signal waits on the phone, marked "not sent yet", and sends by itself when signal comes back, dated when you tapped it. The app opens with no signal too, along with any neighbourhood you've already opened on that phone.

Before a day somewhere with poor signal, open the neighbourhoods you'll work while you still have it.
